# Puṇṇovāda Sutta (MN 145 (PTS MN iii 267))

**ID:** MN 145 (PTS MN iii 267)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Puṇṇovāda Sutta  
**Title (English, from literature):** Advice to Puṇṇa  
**PTS:** MN iii 267  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul4.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul4.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Puṇṇovāda Sutta* ("Advice to Puṇṇa", MN 145; PTS MN iii 267) is the 145th discourse of the Majjhimanikāya. It recounts the exchange between the Buddha and the monk Puṇṇa (Sanskrit: Pūrṇa), who wishes to depart for Sunāparanta (Śroṇāparāntaka) to practice and propagate the Dhamma [Baruah 2000; Bodhi 2003]. Warning him that the people of Sunāparanta are fierce and violent, the Buddha questions Puṇṇa on how he will react if they verbally abuse, physically assault, or even kill him [Bodhi 2003; Anālayo]. Puṇṇa responds with steadfast equanimity, reflecting at each escalating threat that his assailants are kind for not subjecting him to worse violence [Anālayo]. The discourse also records the Buddha's guidance regarding the cessation of delight (*nandī*) in sensory objects [Shulman 2014], and the Buddha praises Puṇṇa for practicing in accordance with the Dhamma without troubling him over matters of interpretation [Flores 2008].

 The commentary (*Puṇṇovādasuttavaṇṇanā*) elaborates Puṇṇa's background as a merchant from Śūrpāraka and became an influential textual source for regional narratives, including Burmese chronicles [Pranke] and Siamese literature combining the sutta and commentary into footprint pilgrimage lore [Lamotte 1988; Skilling].

- Passage-level parallels: d1 འདུལ་བ་གཞི།  (Vinaya-vastu)
